title: Muttergottesgläschen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 207. Text from Wikisource („Muttergottesgläschen (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: A wagoner's wine cart is stuck fast on the road, and the Mother of God, passing by thirsty, offers to free it for a glass of wine — but he has no glass. She plucks a small white, red-striped bindweed flower shaped like a cup; he fills it, she drinks, and the cart rolls free. The flower is called Muttergottesgläschen, Our Lady's little glass, to this day.

sentences.t: Es hatte einmal ein Fuhrmann seinen Karren, der mit Wein schwer beladen war, festgefahren, so daß er ihn trotz aller Mühe nicht wieder losbringen konnte.
sentences.l: Once a carter had got his cart, which was heavily laden with wine, stuck fast, so that in spite of all his effort he could not get it loose again.
sentences.i: There was once a carter who had got his cart, heavily laden with wine, stuck fast, so that with all his effort he could not free it again.
sentences.n: “hatte … festgefahren” is the pluperfect of festfahren (fest + fahren), literally “to drive stuck” — of a wagon become bogged down. “trotz” takes the genitive (“aller Mühe”), the older, more literary usage; modern German often shifts it to the dative. “losbringen” (los + bringen) = to get loose, to free. “daß” is the 1857 spelling of dass; the ß is kept throughout this edition.

sentences.t: Nun kam gerade die Mutter Gottes des Weges daher, und als sie die Noth des armen Mannes sah, sprach sie zu ihm „ich bin müd und durstig, gib mir ein Glas Wein, und ich will dir deinen Wagen frei machen.“
sentences.l: Now just then the Mother of God came along the way, and when she saw the distress of the poor man, she spoke to him “I am tired and thirsty; give me a glass of wine, and I will make your wagon free.”
sentences.i: Just then the Mother of God came along the way, and when she saw the poor man’s distress, she said to him, “I am tired and thirsty; give me a glass of wine, and I will set your wagon free for you.”
sentences.n: “des Weges … daher” is a genitive of route — along the way, along the road (an older idiom). “die Mutter Gottes,” with genitive Gottes, is Grimm’s standard title for the Virgin Mary — literally “the Mother of God.” “Noth” is the 1857 spelling of Not (distress, need). “müd” is a shortened müde (tired), common in Grimm before a vowel or a light rhythm. Grimm places direct speech straight after “sprach zu ihm,” without a comma or colon. Read “du/dein” throughout as English “you/your.”

sentences.t: „Gerne,“ antwortete der Fuhrmann, „aber ich habe kein Glas, worin ich dir den Wein geben könnte.“
sentences.l: “Gladly,” answered the carter, “but I have no glass in which I could give you the wine.”
sentences.i: “Gladly,” answered the carter, “but I have no glass to give you the wine in.”
sentences.n: “worin” = wherein, in which — a relative adverb the reader will meet again in Grimm. The subjunctive “könnte” carries the softening of a hypothetical — “in which I could give you.”

sentences.t: Da brach die Mutter Gottes ein weißes Blümchen mit rothen Streifen ab, das Feldwinde heißt und einem Glase sehr ähnlich sieht, und reichte es dem Fuhrmann.
sentences.l: Then the Mother of God broke off a little white flower with red stripes, which is called Feldwinde and looks very like a glass, and handed it to the carter.
sentences.i: Then the Mother of God plucked a little white flower with red stripes, called the field bindweed, which looks very like a glass, and passed it to the carter.
sentences.n: “Blümchen” is a diminutive of Blume — a little flower; the -chen ending makes it small and fond, and locks the gender to neuter. “Feldwinde” (Feld + Winde) is the field bindweed, Convolvulus arvensis — a low twining plant whose cupped white flower with faint pink stripes gives the tale its whole point. “brach … ab” is the separable abbrechen (to break off, to pluck). “rothen” has the 1857 -th- (roten); “Streifen” is dative plural after mit.

sentences.t: Er füllte es mit Wein, und die Mutter Gottes trank ihn,
sentences.l: He filled it with wine, and the Mother of God drank it,
sentences.n: “ihn” is masculine accusative and points back to “den Wein” (Wein is masculine): the wine, resolved in English as “it” or “the wine.” The comma at the end is Grimm’s — the sentence runs on into the next thought.

sentences.t: und in dem Augenblick ward der Wagen frei und der Fuhrmann konnte weiter fahren.
sentences.l: and at that moment the wagon became free and the carter could drive on.
sentences.i: and at that moment the wagon was loose, and the carter could drive on.
sentences.n: “ward” is the archaic preterite of werden (became); modern German uses “wurde.” In Grimm it reads simply as a past. “weiter fahren” = to drive on, continue driving (separable weiter-).

sentences.t: Das Blümchen heißt noch immer Muttergottesgläschen.
sentences.l: The little flower is still called Muttergottesgläschen — Our Lady’s Little Glass.
sentences.i: The little flower is still called Muttergottesgläschen, Our Lady’s Little Glass.
sentences.n: “Muttergottesgläschen” is a threefold diminutive compound — Mutter (mother) + Gottes (of God) + Gläschen (little glass, from Glas). The aetiology closes the tale: the flower keeps her name. The same plant was called Feldwinde a moment before, in a botanical register.

glossary.glase: das Glas — glass (dative singular; older -e ending after preposition; here of the drinking-glass the flower resembles)
